newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zairean rebels advance towards main southern city.
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebels advance towards main southern city.

text.p: Aid workers said on Thursday Tutsi rebels battling Zaire's ragged army pushed close to the capital of South Kivu province and nearly 300,000 refugees were on the move.
Zairean soldiers set up roadblocks in panic-stricken Bukavu and controlled movements of people. Officers said they expected heavy military reinforcements from Kinshasa on Thursday.
The refugees are mainly Rwandan and Burundian Hutus fleeing camps in South Kivu and some 10,000 Zaireans facing epidemics and food shortages unless food aid arrives in Bukavu in days.
The aid workers said ethnic Tutsi Banyamulenge fighters reached the town of Nyangezi, 27 kms (17 miles) south of Bukavu, on Wednesday night. It was not clear if the town had fallen.
Unconfirmed reports from Zairean soldiers said Banyamulenge had also seized Kamanyola and Bwegera towns, south of Bukavu.
"The Zairean military informed us that the rebels had reached Nyangezi town last night," an aid worker told Reuters.
Another said: "The Zairean military informed us of the threat of an attack on Bukavu last night, so we had to take security precautions."
More than 30 aid workers spent the night in a U.N. compound in Bukavu following the warning from the Zaireans, they said.

Patrick de Souza, head of the U.N. refugee agency in Bukavu, told Reuters that his organisation was arranging for the relocation of some staff from the city. About 15 Belgian women and children were also set to leave on Friday, diplomats added.
A western diplomat in Bukavu said high-level diplomatic efforts involving the Belgian, French and U.S. governments were underway to try and stop fighting between the army and rebels.
The diplomat said Banyamulenge aimed to empty Rwandan refugee camps in eastern Zaire and seize territory to force the Zairean government to negotiate over their claim to Zairean citizenship.

"They (Banyamulenge) have nearly finished the job," he said. "Now that their troops are in position, they are in a position to negotiate. With recent withdrawals, the Zaireans are in a weaker position."
The fighting, which began last month, has closed the two overland supply routes for South Kivu's half million displaced.
Peter Kessler, spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Nairobi, said close to 300,000 refugees and Zaireans were now on the move outside Uvira and Bukavu cities.

He said the situation however was calm in Goma city near the largest Rwandan refugee camps. Goma, the capital of North Kivu, is outside the Banyamulenge homeland of the South Kivu plateau south of Bukavu.

The Banyamulenge came to Zaire from Rwanda as long ago as the end of the 18th century. They say they are discriminated against and, like Rwanda, deny Zairean accusations that members of Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army are fighting alongside them.

But a Banyamulenge spokesman, while denying any Rwandan role, said on Thursday Rwanda could not be expected not to do anything while fellow Tutsis were saying they were the target of genocide similar to the 1994 genocide by Hutus in Rwanda.
The Banyamulenge advances have surprised aid officials even given the very poor morale and equipment of the Zairean army.
Eastern Zaire has been a powderkeg since the 1994 civil war in Rwanda and genocide sent more than a million Hutus afraid of reprisals for the slaughter into the region and fuelled local rivalries.
Diplomats and aid officials fear Tutsi-dominated armies in Burundi and Rwanda could be drawn into the fighting, sparking a wider conflict in Central Africa's volatile Great Lakes region.
